guides.stage: My foreign family member was arrested
guides.title: When a foreign family member is arrested
guides.lead: Within 48 hours of the arrest, it will be decided whether to request an arrest warrant (구속영장) for detention. If your family member is a foreigner, interpretation, consular notification and immigration issues must also be handled, so first find out which police station they are at.

seo.title: When a Foreign Family Member Is Arrested in Korea: The First 48 Hours, Consular Notification and Lawyer Visits | Jisan Law Foreigner Center
seo.description: What to do right away and what not to do when a foreign family member is arrested in Korea, the 48 hours after arrest and the pre-detention hearing, requesting consular notification, translated warrants, family requests for a lawyer visit, and immigration issues after release.

sections.title: What to do right now
body: If you hear of an arrest, do not panic. Organize things in the following order.
bullets: Find out which police station they are at, who the investigator in charge is, and what they are accused of.
Check your family member's passport, residence card, status of stay and expiry date.
Check whether your family member wants the consulate to be notified, and if so, ask the investigator.
Gather documents showing their address, job and family relationships (lease contract, certificate of employment, family relationship documents).
Request a lawyer visit right away. The spouse, lineal relatives and siblings can also make this request.

sections.title: What not to do
body: The family's actions can work against the arrested person.
bullets: Contacting the victim or accomplices to align stories or push for a settlement.
Removing or deleting phones or documents at home.
Family members explaining the case to the investigator on the person's behalf without knowing the details.
Hurriedly leaving for your home country. This can be seen as a risk of flight.

sections.title: The 48 hours after arrest
body: To detain an arrested suspect, an arrest warrant for detention must be requested within 48 hours of the arrest, and if it is not requested, the suspect must be released immediately (Criminal Procedure Act Article 200-2(5) and Article 200-4). If a warrant is requested, a judge questions the suspect directly, usually by the day after the request.

At the pre-detention hearing (영장실질심사), the judge considers whether the person has a fixed residence and whether there is a risk of flight or destruction of evidence. Foreigners are easily seen as likely to leave the country, so it is important to show with evidence their housing, job, family and how long they have lived in Korea. If the person has no lawyer, the judge appoints a court-appointed defense counsel.

sections.title: Additional procedures for foreigners
body: When the police arrest or detain a foreigner, they must tell the person that they can meet and communicate with consular officers and can ask for the consulate to be informed of the arrest, and if requested, must notify the consulate without delay (Police Investigation Rules Article 91). This is also a right under Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. For some countries, notification is required under a treaty regardless of the person's wishes.

A translation must be attached when executing a warrant, such as an arrest warrant, or when giving a list of seized items (Rules on Criminal Investigation Article 218). During questioning, the person must be given interpretation in a language they understand.

sections.title: What happens next
body: If the person is detained, the next decision is made within 10 days at the police stage and within 10 days at the prosecutor stage at the Public Prosecution Service, with extensions if needed. Even if they are released without detention, the investigation continues and they may be banned from leaving Korea.

Once a sentence becomes final, immigration issues follow. A person released after being sentenced to imprisonment without labor or a heavier sentence can become subject to deportation, and prison wardens must notify the immigration office of foreigners whose release has been decided. That is why preparing for immigration issues must begin at the criminal trial stage.

sections.title: How Jisan Law can help
body: Jisan Law visits the arrested person to hear their circumstances, and checks that consular notification and interpretation were properly provided. We attend the pre-detention hearing to explain, with evidence of housing and ties to Korea, that detention is not necessary, and we also sit in on questioning during detention. We can consult with the family in English or Chinese.
The time right after the arrest is the most urgent. If a lawyer visit is needed, call us first at 02-6951-4097. We answer 24 hours a day, including weekends and public holidays.

faqs.q: Can family members visit at the police station?
faqs.a: Visits to a police lockup have set hours and procedures, and may be restricted depending on the investigation. Lawyer visits are separate from family visits, so it is safer to discuss the case through the lawyer.

faqs.q: If they are detained, will they be sent straight back to their home country?
faqs.a: While criminal proceedings are ongoing, the person usually must stand trial, so they are not removed immediately. After the criminal proceedings end, whether they will be deported is decided in the immigration procedure.

faqs.q: Can they be released on bail?
faqs.a: After indictment, bail can be requested. For foreigners, the risk of flight is often the issue, so it is important to prepare evidence of housing, family, employment and a personal guarantee.

guides.stage: I have not been paid my wages or severance pay
guides.title: When you have not been paid your wages or severance pay
guides.lead: Foreign workers can receive payment for their work regardless of their status of stay. If you have a departure date, it is important to plan the order of the petition, lawsuit and provisional attachment around that date.

seo.title: What to Do When a Foreign Worker Is Not Paid Wages or Severance Pay in Korea | Jisan Law Foreigner Center
seo.description: What a foreign worker in Korea should do right away and what not to do when wages or severance pay are not paid, petitions to the Labor Office and worries about immigration reporting, Departure Guarantee Insurance, the stricter penalties from October 8, 2026, and lawsuits and substitute payments before and after leaving Korea.

sections.title: What to do right now
body: Whether before or after leaving the company, secure the following materials first.
bullets: Save your employment contract, pay slips and the bank statements showing your salary deposits as photos or PDFs.
Collect records showing your working hours (entry records, photos of work schedules, messages).
Do not delete messages with your boss or manager about your pay. Take screenshots.
Check your expiry date and planned departure date.
If you work under the Employment Permit System, check whether you are enrolled in Departure Guarantee Insurance and the amount.

sections.title: What not to do
body: Many people lose money owed to them by trying to settle things in a hurry.
bullets: Signing a document saying you do not want the employer punished before you have received all the money.
Signing a confirmation that you have received the full amount.
Taking company property or touching the company's bank account.
For workers under the Employment Permit System, starting work somewhere else right away without permission.

sections.title: Will reporting cause problems with my stay?
body: Court precedent holds that even a foreigner without work authorization can receive payment for work already done and industrial accident insurance benefits (Supreme Court Decision 94Nu12067, September 15, 1995). A labor inspector's investigation of unpaid wages is one of the duties in which the duty to notify immigration can be waived when helping the victim is found to come first (Enforcement Rules of the Immigration Act Article 70-2(5)).
However, the official in charge decides whether to notify. If your visa status is uncertain, get advice before filing a petition and decide on the order and method.

sections.title: What happens next
body: If you have left the job, the company must pay your wages and severance pay within 14 days. If it does not, file a petition with the regional employment and labor office and appear for the labor inspector's investigation to have the unpaid amount confirmed. From October 8, 2026, the penalty became heavier: employers who fail to pay wages and retirement payments face imprisonment of up to 5 years or a fine of up to KRW 50 million (Labor Standards Act Article 107). This offense cannot be prosecuted if the worker does not want punishment, so the timing of signing a statement that you do not want punishment (처벌불원서) during a settlement is important.

If you still cannot get the money through the Labor Office, we create an enforceable basis through a civil lawsuit or payment order and provisionally attach the company's assets. If the company has gone bankrupt or is found unable to pay, you can apply for the substitute payment (대지급금).

Workers under the Employment Permit System mainly receive severance pay through Departure Guarantee Insurance. The insurance money is paid within 14 days after departure and expires if not claimed within 3 years. If the payment seems less than the statutory severance pay, the difference should be examined.

sections.title: How Jisan Law can help
body: Jisan Law calculates the money owed to you based on documents and plans the order of the petition, lawsuit and provisional attachment around your stay schedule. We go with you when you appear at the Labor Office to help with interpretation and your statement, and continue the lawsuit and enforcement as your representative even after you leave Korea. Consultations are available in English and Chinese.
If your departure is close and time is short, contact us first at 02-6951-4097.

faqs.q: Can I still get wages from several years ago?
faqs.a: In principle, wage claims expire by prescription if not exercised for 3 years (Labor Standards Act Article 49). For older unpaid wages, start by organizing by date when each payment was due.

faqs.q: My boss is threatening to report my visa problems.
faqs.a: Threatening someone with their immigration status in response to a demand for unpaid wages can itself be a problem. Keep the threatening messages, and get advice together with your visa status to decide how to respond.

faqs.q: I was paid only in cash, not into a bank account. Can I prove it?
faqs.a: Even if you were paid in cash, you can prove that you worked and the wages promised through attendance records, coworkers' statements, messages with your boss, photos of you at work and so on. Collect every piece of evidence you can.

guides.title: When you receive a notice to appear about cancellation of your stay permit
guides.lead: If the immigration office has notified you to appear regarding the cancellation of your stay permit, this is your chance to explain your circumstances before a decision is made. Check each reason stated in the notice and bring the evidence you have prepared.

seo.title: Notice to Appear About Stay Permit Cancellation in Korea: Preparing Your Statement | Jisan Law Foreigner Center
seo.description: What to check in the notice when you are asked to appear about the cancellation of your stay permit or permanent residency in Korea, the evidence to prepare beforehand, what to say when stating your opinion, and administrative appeals, lawsuits and stays of execution after a cancellation decision.

sections.title: What to check in the notice
body: When the Minister of Justice intends to cancel or change a stay permit or other permit, the foreigner may be called to appear and give their opinion if necessary, and must be informed of the reasons for the intended cancellation and the date, time and place at least 7 days before the hearing (Immigration Act Article 89(2) and (3)).
bullets: Which provision (which item of Article 89(1)) is cited as the reason
When the document or action in question took place
The date and place to appear, and the documents to bring
For permanent residency, which ground under Article 89-2 applies

sections.title: Common grounds for cancellation
body: The law sets out five grounds for cancellation: the guarantor withdraws the guarantee or no longer exists; it turns out the permit was obtained by false or improper means; the permit conditions were breached; circumstances have changed so seriously that the permit cannot be maintained; or the violation of law is serious or a legitimate official order from an immigration officer was violated (Immigration Act Article 89(1)).

In practice, the most common issues are suspicion that application documents were untrue and criminal penalties. For document issues, the question is whether you intended to deceive from the start or whether your circumstances changed later. Permanent residency (F-5) can be cancelled only in narrower, specified cases, such as a final sentence of imprisonment with or without labor of 2 years or more, or final sentences adding up to 3 years or more within the last 5 years (Article 89-2).

sections.title: Evidence to prepare before you appear
body: The evidence you need depends on the reason. If the reason is that documents were untrue, you need evidence showing how the documents were prepared and what the actual situation was at the time. If the reason is a serious violation of law, prepare the judgment together with records of compensation to the victim, settlement and your life since.

Your long life in Korea, Korean family members and children, and employment and tax records can be used for any ground to argue that the decision is too harsh. Organize the evidence in date order, and attach translations to documents in foreign languages.

sections.title: What to keep in mind when stating your opinion
body: If you do not fully understand a question, ask for an interpreter and ask again. Say you do not know when you do not know, and do not answer with guesses. When your statement is finished, ask for what was written to be read back to you, and ask for anything recorded differently to be corrected.

If you have a reason you cannot appear, contact them in advance to ask for a different date, and it is a good idea to also submit a written opinion. If you fail to appear without contacting them, you lose your chance to give your opinion.

sections.title: If a cancellation decision is issued
body: You can challenge a cancellation decision through an administrative appeal or administrative lawsuit within 90 days of the day you learned of the decision. A departure order is often issued together to people whose stay permits are cancelled, so you must apply for a stay of execution within the departure deadline.

If your permanent residency is cancelled, you can apply for a general status of stay if you need to keep staying in Korea and meet the requirements. If this application is accepted, you are no longer subject to a departure order, so it should be considered together with challenging the cancellation.

sections.title: How Jisan Law can help
body: Jisan Law reviews the notice together with your past application documents, organizes the grounds at issue, and prepares a written opinion and supporting evidence. We practice with likely questions in advance, and if a decision is issued, we continue with the administrative appeal, lawsuit and stay of execution. If your hearing date is close, contact us at 02-6951-4097.

faqs.q: I am worried that I will be detained as soon as I appear.
faqs.a: Appearing does not in itself mean detention. However, if grounds for deportation are also at issue in your case, detention is possible, so check the nature of the case before appearing and leave the necessary documents and contact details with your family.

faqs.q: Can a lawyer appear with me?
faqs.a: It is a good idea to check with the office in advance about appearing with a representative or submitting a written opinion. The procedure may vary depending on the office.

guides.title: How a fine or suspended sentence affects your stay
guides.lead: A fine, a suspended sentence and a prison sentence each affect your stay differently. If you know what each possible outcome means for your stay before your criminal case is decided, you can decide what to aim for in the investigation and trial.

seo.title: Fines, Suspended Sentences, Prison Sentences and Your Visa in Korea | Jisan Law Foreigner Center
seo.description: What happens to a foreigner's stay in Korea after a suspended indictment, a fine, a suspended sentence or a prison sentence: imprisonment without labor or heavier and deportation, cancellation of stay permits, standards for cancelling permanent residency, requesting a formal trial after a summary order, and the effect on naturalization reviews.

sections.title: Outcome by outcome
body: The following is based mainly on the standards set by law. The actual immigration decision is made by the immigration office after looking at how the case happened and your circumstances in Korea.
bullets: Suspended indictment (기소유예): this is not a criminal penalty, so it does not count as 'imprisonment without labor or a heavier sentence', which is a ground for deportation. However, it remains in investigation history records, which can be checked when needed for a stay or naturalization permit (Act on the Lapse of Criminal Sentences Article 6(1)(6)).

Fine: it is not included in 'imprisonment without labor or a heavier sentence', which is a ground for deportation, but it counts against you in extension, change of status, permanent residency and naturalization reviews, and if the violation is serious, it can be a ground for cancelling your stay permit.
Suspended sentence (집행유예): this is still a sentence of imprisonment with or without labor, so the ground for deportation can become an issue.

Prison sentence (실형): you can become subject to deportation when released after serving your sentence, and prison wardens must notify the immigration office of foreigners whose release has been decided.
Permanent residents: permanent residency can be cancelled only in specified cases, such as a final sentence of imprisonment with or without labor of 2 years or more.

sections.title: Setting your goal at the investigation stage
body: For Korean nationals, the difference between a fine and a suspended indictment may not seem large, but for foreigners it makes a big difference at the next immigration review. So even if you admit the allegations, it is important to fully submit evidence of compensation to the victim, settlement, remorse and your life in Korea at the investigation stage.
When the prosecutor decides on the outcome, the effect on your stay can be considered as one of the circumstances. Describe your family, job and long life in Korea specifically in a written opinion.

sections.title: If you received a summary order, check the 7 days
body: Cases punishable by fines often end with a summary order (약식명령) without a trial. You can request a formal trial within 7 days of receiving the summary order (Criminal Procedure Act Article 453). In a formal trial, you can dispute the amount of the fine or seek a suspended sentencing (선고유예).

A suspended sentencing is a system under which, when imposing imprisonment with or without labor of 1 year or less, suspension of qualifications or a fine, the court defers pronouncing the sentence if the defendant shows clear remorse (Criminal Act Article 59). It is not available to people with a prior conviction of suspension of qualifications or heavier. It is an option worth considering in cases where your stay is at stake.

sections.title: How to explain your immigration circumstances at trial
body: When deciding a sentence, the court considers the defendant's circumstances and what happened after the offense. For a foreign defendant, we explain with evidence that the sentence may lead to deportation or refusal of stay, and how family members in Korea would be affected. However, immigration circumstances alone do not make the sentence lighter, so compensating the victim and showing remorse come first.

sections.title: How Jisan Law can help
body: Jisan Law looks at the criminal case and your stay together. At the investigation stage, we work to reduce the outcome through practice for questioning, sitting in on questioning and written opinions, and at trial we organize your immigration circumstances as sentencing materials. If the immigration office starts an investigation or issues a decision after the outcome, we continue on to statements of opinion, objections and administrative lawsuits. If you have received a summary order, contact us at 02-6951-4097 before the 7 days pass.

faqs.q: How large a fine will prevent my visa extension?
faqs.a: The law does not set a threshold amount for fines. Many of the standards used in practice are not public, and decisions vary from case to case, so rather than trusting numbers circulating online, it is better to prepare evidence of how the case happened and of your life in Korea.

faqs.q: Do penalties I received in my home country also matter?
faqs.a: When questioning a foreign suspect, the police are required to ask whether they have a criminal record abroad (Rules on Criminal Investigation Article 216). Immigration reviews also sometimes require overseas criminal record documents, so answer truthfully.

guides.title: When you receive a request to appear for an immigration violation review or a notice to pay an immigration fine
guides.lead: If it is confirmed that you overstayed or worked without permission, the immigration office will investigate and review your case. Your statement when you appear is kept in a statement record, and if you receive a notice to pay an immigration fine (범칙금 통고서) and do not pay within 15 days of receiving it, the case may be referred for prosecution and move into criminal proceedings.

seo.title: Immigration Violation Review and Notices to Pay an Immigration Fine in Korea | Jisan Law Foreigner Center
seo.description: When you receive a notice to pay an immigration fine in Korea for overstaying, activities outside your status of stay or changing workplaces without permission: the 15-day payment deadline, what happens if you do not pay, the link to departure orders, and how immigration violations are referred for prosecution.
keywords: notice to pay immigration fine Korea
activities outside status of stay Korea

sections.title: What is a notice to pay an immigration fine?
body: If the head of the immigration office confirms an offense after investigating an immigration violation, they can notify the person in writing to pay an amount equivalent to a fine, called an immigration fine (범칙금), to a designated place (Immigration Act Article 102(1)). If you pay the immigration fine, the case is closed without going to criminal trial.

Immigration violation cases cannot be prosecuted without a referral from the head of the immigration office (Article 101). However, if the investigation shows that the case appears to warrant imprisonment without labor or a heavier sentence, it must be referred immediately without a notice (Article 102(3)).

sections.title: When you appear for questioning
body: If needed for the investigation, the office will ask you to appear for questioning and record your statement in a statement record. The record must be read to you or shown to you, and you must be asked whether anything was written incorrectly. If you ask for additions or changes, those must also be recorded. The statements of a person who does not understand Korean must be interpreted by an interpreter (Immigration Act Article 48).

Bring evidence showing how the violation happened (messages with your company, medical certificates, application records), and do not answer with guesses when you do not know. This statement record becomes the basic material for deciding on the immigration fine, a departure order or deportation.

sections.title: You must pay within 15 days
body: When you receive the notice, you must pay the immigration fine within 15 days. If you do not, the head of the office must refer the case for prosecution. If you pay before the referral, the case will not be referred (Article 105(1) and (2)). Once the case is referred, criminal proceedings begin, and a record of a criminal fine may remain.
If you dispute the amount of the immigration fine or the violation itself, get advice before paying. Paying the immigration fine may be taken to mean that you accept the violation.

sections.title: The immigration fine and departure measures are separate
body: Paying the immigration fine does not end the immigration issue. If the head of the office considers departure measures appropriate after the notice, a departure order can be issued (Article 68(1)(5)). Depending on how serious the violation is, deportation proceedings may also be started, and if a deportation order has been issued, the case is not referred even if the immigration fine is not paid (Article 105(3)).

Overstaying and engaging in activities of another status without permission are acts punishable by law with imprisonment of up to 3 years or a fine of up to KRW 30 million (Article 94), and changing workplaces without permission is punishable by imprisonment of up to 1 year or a fine of up to KRW 10 million (Article 95). The notice procedure is a way to settle these cases without a trial.

sections.title: If you want to continue your stay
body: In some cases you can pay the immigration fine and continue your stay, but the violation record will be considered at your next extension or change of status review. If you organize now the evidence showing how the violation happened (delayed company documents, illness, lack of information, etc.), it will be easier to explain later.

If you have received a departure order, check the departure deadline and how to challenge it right away. Whether you leave under a departure order or are deported makes a big difference when you want to enter Korea again.

sections.title: How Jisan Law can help
body: Jisan Law reviews the notice and the investigation records and decides whether it is better to pay the immigration fine or to dispute the violation. If a departure order or deportation proceedings follow, we also handle statements of opinion, objections and administrative lawsuits. If you have received a notice, contact us before the 15 days pass.

faqs.q: Can I pay the immigration fine in installments?
faqs.a: The law has a provision on provisional payment (Immigration Act Article 102(2)), but whether installment payments are possible depends on the office's practice. If it is hard to pay within the deadline, contact the office in advance.

faqs.q: I overstayed because of my company. Is it still my responsibility?
faqs.a: The duty to apply for an extension of stay lies with the foreigner. However, circumstances such as the company not providing documents may be taken into account in the outcome or later reviews, so keep evidence.

guides.title: When an E-9 worker wants to change companies
guides.lead: Workers under the Employment Permit System (E-9) can change workplaces only if there is a reason, and must apply within 1 month of the date their employment contract ended. Even if your employer does not agree, check whether you can apply because the reason is not your fault.

seo.title: Changing Companies on an E-9 Visa: Reasons and Deadlines for a Workplace Change in Korea | Jisan Law Foreigner Center
seo.description: When a worker under the Employment Permit System in Korea wants to change workplaces: reasons for a change, when you can apply without your employer's consent, the 1-month and 3-month deadlines, the number of changes allowed, what not to do while applying, and dismissal and remedy applications.

sections.title: What to check first
body: If you are thinking about a workplace change, check the following before you quit.
bullets: When your employment contract ends, and whether your employer has said they will not renew it
Whether you have evidence of the company's fault, such as unpaid wages, assault or problems with your housing
How many times and for what reasons you have changed workplaces so far
How much of your employment period is left (3 years after entry, plus any extended period through re-employment)

sections.title: When you do not need your employer's consent
body: You can apply for a workplace change when the employer ends the contract or refuses to renew it for a legitimate reason, when the company suspends operations or closes, when the employment permit is cancelled or hiring is restricted, or when the Minister of Employment and Labor has announced that it is hard to keep working for reasons that are not the worker's fault, such as violations of working conditions or unfair treatment (Act on the Employment of Foreign Workers Article 25(1)).

Whether your situation falls under the public notice must be shown with evidence. Collect materials such as bank records showing unpaid wages, medical certificates for injuries, photos of your housing and recordings of verbal abuse, and if needed, it helps to first file a petition with the Labor Office or a police report.

sections.title: Deadlines and number of changes
body: You must apply for a change within 1 month of the date your employment contract ended, and obtain permission to change workplace to a new company within 3 months of the date you applied. If these deadlines pass, you must leave Korea. If you could not apply because of a work-related injury, illness, pregnancy or childbirth, the period is counted from the day that reason ends.

In principle, you can change workplaces up to 3 times during the first 3 years and up to 2 times during a period extended by re-employment. Changes for reasons that are not your fault are not counted, so checking the reasons for past changes may change the number of changes you have left.

sections.title: What not to do
body: Mistakes during the change process can lead to losing your stay.
bullets: Starting work at a new company before obtaining permission to change workplace. This violates the Immigration Act and can lead to punishment and deportation.
Stopping going to work without saying anything. You may be reported for workplace desertion.
Paying a broker to introduce you to a company.

sections.title: If you were dismissed, also take care of the following
body: At a workplace with 5 or more regular employees, you can challenge a dismissal without a justifiable reason as invalid. Apply to the Regional Labor Relations Commission for remedy within 3 months of the date of dismissal, and if you disagree with the decision, apply to the National Labor Relations Commission for a review within 10 days of receiving the written decision (Labor Standards Act Articles 28 and 31). If you were dismissed without 30 days' notice, you can claim at least 30 days' ordinary wages (Article 26).

Even if you apply for remedy, the deadline for a workplace change application (1 month from the end of the contract) runs separately. You must prepare both procedures at the same time to avoid losing your stay.

sections.title: How Jisan Law can help
body: Jisan Law organizes the reasons for the change and the evidence to determine whether you can apply without your employer's consent, and if there are unpaid wages or assault, we also file a petition with the Labor Office and a criminal complaint. If you were dismissed, we prepare the application for remedy to the Labor Relations Commission and the workplace change application together within the deadlines. Consultations are available in English and Chinese.

faqs.q: My boss says he will report me for workplace desertion.
faqs.a: Keep a record of why you stopped going to work and of your attempts to contact the company. If the reason is unpaid wages or unfair treatment, that evidence becomes the basis for explaining that it was not desertion.

faqs.q: What happens if I cannot find a new company within 3 months?
faqs.a: If you do not obtain permission to change workplace within 3 months of applying, you must leave Korea (Act on the Employment of Foreign Workers Article 25(3)). If there is a reason set by law, such as illness or a work-related injury, the period is calculated differently, so prepare supporting documents.

guides.title: For marriage migrants considering divorce from a Korean spouse
guides.lead: For marriage migrants, divorce is both a family issue and an immigration issue. If the Korean spouse is mainly responsible for the breakdown of the marriage, there is a way to stay after the divorce, so organize your evidence before deciding how to divorce.

seo.title: Divorce for Marriage Migrants in Korea: Staying After Divorce, F-6 Item (c) and Custody | Jisan Law Foreigner Center
seo.description: Immigration issues that marriage migrants considering divorce from a Korean spouse should know: the main responsibility for the breakdown of the marriage and F-6 item (c), raising children and F-6 item (b), special stay rules for domestic violence victims, and the difference between divorce by agreement and judicial divorce.

sections.title: What to organize first
body: Before deciding to divorce, check the following.
bullets: Your current status of stay and its expiry date
Why and when the marriage became difficult (violence, leaving home, failure to pay living expenses, an affair, etc.)
Evidence showing those reasons (messages, police reports, medical certificates, photos, money transfer records)
Whether you have children with your Korean spouse, and who is raising them now
Property you built up together and property in each spouse's name

sections.title: Ways to continue your stay
body: There are three types of marriage migrant (F-6) status. Item (a) (가목) is for the spouse of a Korean national; item (b) (나목) is for a parent raising a child born from a marriage with a Korean national; and item (c) (다목) is for a person who cannot maintain the marriage because of the spouse's death or disappearance or other reasons they are not responsible for.

The Supreme Court interprets 'reasons they are not responsible for' in item (c) as cases where the Korean spouse is mainly responsible for the breakdown of the marriage. The foreign spouse does not have to be completely without fault (Supreme Court Decision 2018Du66869, July 4, 2019). If you are raising a child, item (b) is also considered.

sections.title: Divorce by agreement and judicial divorce
body: A divorce by agreement (협의이혼) is quick, but there is no record of whose responsibility the breakdown was. To stay under item (c), you must prove that responsibility separately, which can be difficult. If the court recognizes the Korean spouse's responsibility in a judicial divorce (재판상 이혼), that finding is in principle respected in immigration reviews and lawsuits.

A divorce from a Korean spouse who lives in Korea is governed by Korean law (Act on Private International Law Article 66). Along with the divorce, you can claim compensation for emotional distress, division of property, designation of the person with parental authority and the custodial parent, and child support.

sections.title: Children and property
body: If the child lives in Korea, Korean courts can handle cases on parental authority and custody (Act on Private International Law Article 59). The fact that you are actually raising the child is important both in designating the custodial parent and for marriage migrant (F-6) item (b) status. Collect evidence showing who took care of the child's school, hospital visits and living expenses.

You can claim division of property built up together during the marriage even if it is in your spouse's name, and you can claim compensation for emotional distress from the spouse responsible for the breakdown of the marriage. If there is a risk that your spouse will hide or dispose of property, we first consider a provisional attachment or provisional injunction.

sections.title: If there is violence, safety comes first
body: If there is domestic violence, report it to the police and get help from a counseling center or shelter. A marriage migrant who has an investigation, trial or protection procedure in progress because of domestic violence can receive extensions of stay until the procedure ends (Immigration Act Article 25-2). Police report records and medical certificates are used both for your stay and in the divorce lawsuit.

sections.title: How Jisan Law can help
body: Jisan Law looks at the divorce lawsuit and your immigration situation together. We organize evidence showing responsibility for the breakdown of the marriage and pursue a judicial divorce, and we prepare your application for an extension of stay or change of status in step with the divorce proceedings. If your stay is refused, we continue with an administrative appeal and lawsuit based on the divorce judgment. Consultations are available in English and Chinese.

faqs.q: My husband filed for divorce first. Is that bad for me?
faqs.a: What matters is not who filed first but whom the court finds responsible for the breakdown of the marriage. Submit evidence of your spouse's responsibility in your answer and counterclaim. You must file your answer within 30 days of receiving the complaint.

faqs.q: What if my period of stay ends during the divorce lawsuit?
faqs.a: You must apply for an extension of stay before it expires, with documents showing that the lawsuit is in progress. Whether it is granted and in what form depends on the office's judgment, so prepare in advance.

guides.title: Settling your deposit and money owed to you before leaving Korea
guides.lead: If you have to leave Korea because your period of stay is ending or you received a departure order, and money is still owed to you, there are things to do before you leave. If you arrange a representative and documents, the procedures can continue even after you leave.

seo.title: How to Settle Deposits, Wages and Severance Pay Before Leaving Korea | Jisan Law Foreigner Center
seo.description: How to settle unpaid housing deposits, wages, severance pay and Departure Guarantee Insurance before leaving Korea: orders for registration of lease rights, petitions to the Labor Office, powers of attorney and overseas bank accounts, lawsuits and enforcement after departure, and security for litigation costs.
keywords: registration of lease rights foreigner Korea

sections.title: Checklist before leaving Korea
body: Once your departure date is set, check the following one by one.
bullets: Whether you have received your lease deposit back, and if not, whether you have applied for an order for registration of lease rights
Whether you have unpaid wages or severance pay, and whether you have filed a petition with the Labor Office
If you work under the Employment Permit System, your Departure Guarantee Insurance application and the account to receive it
Evidence of other money owed to you, such as money you lent to others or money lost to fraud
When to close your Korean phone number and bank account

sections.title: For deposits, register first
body: If you move your registered residence or leave Korea without receiving your deposit, you may lose protection for that home. If your lease has ended and you have not received your deposit, apply for an order for registration of lease rights before leaving and confirm that the registration has been made (Housing Lease Protection Act Article 3-3). After that, your priority over the deposit is maintained even if you leave Korea.
If you have agreed on a return date with the landlord, keep it in a text message or in writing, and decide which account the deposit will be paid into.

sections.title: Wages and severance pay
body: When you leave a job, the company must pay your wages and severance pay within 14 days. If you file a petition with the Labor Office before leaving Korea and have the unpaid wages confirmed, you can use this for a lawsuit or a substitute payment application even after you leave. In principle, Departure Guarantee Insurance is paid within 14 days after departure and must be claimed within 3 years.

sections.title: You can still sue after leaving Korea
body: If you appoint a lawyer as your litigation representative, the lawsuit and enforcement can continue after you leave. Prepare a power of attorney, copies of your identity documents, your overseas contact details and the account to receive money before you leave. The verification procedures (such as notarization) needed when sending documents from abroad differ by country.

A plaintiff with no address in Korea may be ordered, at the other party's request, to provide security for litigation costs (Civil Procedure Act Article 117). We take this into account when planning the litigation strategy.

sections.title: Useful public help lines
body: Apart from a lawyer's advice, you can get general information from public help lines. You can contact the Ministry of Justice Immigration Contact Center (외국인종합안내센터, dial 1345 in Korea with no area code) for stay and visa procedures, the Ministry of Employment and Labor Customer Counseling Center (dial 1350 with no area code) for labor issues such as unpaid wages, and the Korea Legal Aid Corporation (132) for everyday legal advice.

If you have already received a decision or are in a dispute with a deadline, such as a lawsuit or objection, general information alone may not be enough. First check the deadline stated in your documents, and also get advice from a lawyer.

sections.title: How Jisan Law can help
body: Jisan Law organizes what must be done before you leave, such as lease registration, petitions to the Labor Office and provisional attachments, according to your departure date, and continues the lawsuit and enforcement as your representative after you leave. Consultations are available in English and Chinese.

faqs.q: I received a departure order. Can I stay longer because of a lawsuit?
faqs.a: A pending lawsuit can be considered when you apply to postpone the departure deadline or extend your stay, but it does not automatically give you permission to stay. If you have a representative, the lawsuit can continue even after you leave.

faqs.q: If I close my Korean bank account, can I not receive the money?
faqs.a: Money can be sent to an overseas account, but this involves fees and time. If money is still owed to you, it is a good idea to decide when to close your account together with your representative.

moreFaqs.q: What is the difference between a departure order and a deportation order?
moreFaqs.a: A departure order (출국명령) is a decision telling you to leave on your own within a set deadline (within 30 days of the issue date), while a deportation order (강제퇴거명령) is a decision under which the state removes you directly (Immigration Act Article 68; Enforcement Rules Article 65; Article 62). If you leave after receiving a deportation order, you may be banned from entering Korea until 5 years have passed (Article 11(1)(6)). The ways to challenge them also differ: for a deportation order, you can file an objection with the Minister of Justice within 7 days of receiving the order.

moreFaqs.q: Can I stay in Korea while my administrative appeal or lawsuit is pending?
moreFaqs.a: Filing an appeal or lawsuit does not in itself suspend the decision (Administrative Appeals Act Article 30(1); Administrative Litigation Act Article 23(1)). To stay while you challenge it, you must apply for a stay of execution within the departure deadline and get a decision. For a stay of execution, you must show harm that would be hard to undo and an urgent need, so prepare evidence of circumstances such as family, medical treatment or studies.

moreFaqs.q: Can I go back to my home country first and file a lawsuit later?
moreFaqs.a: If you appoint a lawyer as your representative, you can file and pursue a lawsuit after leaving Korea. However, depending on the type of decision, there is room for the court to find that you no longer have an interest to be gained from the lawsuit once you have left, and coming back may also become more difficult. It is safer to check the possibility of a lawsuit and a stay of execution before you leave.

moreFaqs.q: My period of stay has already expired. Can I keep staying?
moreFaqs.a: Staying beyond your period of stay without permission to extend it is punishable by imprisonment of up to 3 years or a fine of up to KRW 30 million, and is a ground for deportation (Immigration Act Article 94(17) and Article 46(1)(8)). The longer you wait, the worse it gets, so check right away what procedures are available in your current situation.

moreFaqs.q: The immigration office has asked me to appear. What should I say?
moreFaqs.a: First find out why you are being called (an investigation of a violation, or a hearing on cancellation of your stay permit). Your statement when you appear is kept in a statement record, which must be read to you or shown to you, and you must be asked whether anything needs correcting (Immigration Act Article 48). Explain what happened truthfully, do not answer with guesses, and bring evidence showing your circumstances.

moreFaqs.q: How can I find out whether I am subject to an entry ban and until when?
moreFaqs.a: The law provides that entry can be banned for people who left after receiving a deportation order less than 5 years ago, among others, and the actual period depends on the reason. In many cases the person concerned checks by contacting the immigration office, and the Immigration Contact Center (1345) can tell you how to inquire.

moreFaqs.q: My family member is in an immigration detention center. Is there a way to get them out?
moreFaqs.a: The detained person, their family or a guarantor can apply to the Immigration Detention Committee for temporary release from detention, and if granted, conditions such as a deposit of up to KRW 20 million and restrictions on residence must be followed (Immigration Act Article 65). If the detention itself is unjust, you can request a review, and the Committee decides within 3 weeks (Enforcement Decree Article 70). If a deportation order was also issued, check the 7-day deadline for an objection as well.

moreFaqs.q: Does a record remain even if my case ends in a suspended indictment or a decision not to refer it to prosecutors?
moreFaqs.a: These are not criminal penalties, so they are not part of your criminal record, but a police decision not to refer the case and a prosecutor's decision not to indict remain in investigation history records (Act on the Lapse of Criminal Sentences Article 2(6)). These records can be checked when needed for a foreigner's naturalization, restoration of nationality or stay permit (Article 6(1)(6) of the same Act). So it is good to keep materials explaining what happened along with the decision.

moreFaqs.q: If I am punished for drunk driving or a sexual crime, will I receive a departure order?
moreFaqs.a: Departure orders and deportation are decided by looking at the type of criminal outcome together with your circumstances in Korea. If you are sentenced to imprisonment without labor or a heavier sentence and released, you can become subject to deportation, and even with a fine, if the violation is serious, your stay permit can be cancelled and a departure order may follow (Immigration Act Articles 46, 89 and 68). You need to prepare for the effect on your stay from the investigation stage.

moreFaqs.q: Should I contact the consulate for my arrested foreign family member?
moreFaqs.a: If the arrested person wishes, the police must notify the consulate of the arrest without delay (Police Investigation Rules Article 91). For some countries, notification is made under a treaty regardless of the person's wishes. Family members can also contact the embassy directly, but it is safer to discuss the details of the case through the defense lawyer.

moreFaqs.q: Will I be fired if I report that I was not paid?
moreFaqs.a: An employer cannot dismiss or treat a worker unfavorably because the worker reported a violation of the Labor Standards Act to the Ministry of Employment and Labor or a labor inspector, and employers who do so are punished (Labor Standards Act Articles 104 and 110). Keep records of conversations and any changes in how you are treated before and after reporting.

moreFaqs.q: Can undocumented foreigners also report workplace injuries or crimes?
moreFaqs.a: Yes. Court precedent holds that foreigners without work authorization can also receive industrial accident insurance benefits (Supreme Court Decision 94Nu12067, September 15, 1995), and crime victims can file criminal complaints regardless of their status of stay. When helping the victim comes first, such as in a criminal investigation or an investigation of unpaid wages, public officials may be exempt from the duty to notify immigration (Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Act Article 92-2), but the official in charge decides, so get advice before reporting.

moreFaqs.q: My boss says foreigners are not covered by industrial accident insurance.
moreFaqs.a: In principle, industrial accident insurance applies to all businesses that employ workers and does not distinguish by nationality (Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act Article 6). Even if the company will not file for you, the worker can apply directly to the Korea Workers' Compensation and Welfare Service. The right to receive insurance benefits must be exercised within 3 years (5 years for disability and survivors' benefits, etc.).

moreFaqs.q: I am on an E-9 visa and have already changed workplaces once. Can I change again?
moreFaqs.a: In principle, you can change up to 3 times during the first 3 years and up to 2 times during a period extended by re-employment, and changes for reasons that are not your fault are not counted (Act on the Employment of Foreign Workers Article 25(4)). Also check the deadline: you must apply within 1 month of the date your contract ended.

moreFaqs.q: My foreign spouse went back to their home country and I cannot reach them. Can I get a divorce?
moreFaqs.a: If you, as the person filing, and your minor children live in Korea, or if one of you lives in Korea and the place you last lived together was Korea, you can file for divorce in a Korean court (Act on Private International Law Article 56). If the other spouse's address is unknown or service abroad is difficult, the case can proceed by service by publication (Civil Procedure Act Article 194).

moreFaqs.q: Can I claim compensation for emotional distress, division of property and custody in an international divorce?
moreFaqs.a: Yes. The applicable law depends on nationality and where you live, and if there is a Korean spouse living in Korea, the divorce is governed by Korean law (Act on Private International Law Article 66). If the child lives in Korea, Korean courts can also handle parental authority and custody cases (Article 59). If the other spouse's assets are abroad, enforcement methods must be considered separately.

moreFaqs.q: Can foreigners have their jeonse deposit protected?
moreFaqs.a: Yes. Alien registration and reports of change of residence replace resident registration and move-in reports (Immigration Act Article 88-2(2)), so once you move in and complete the report, you gain the right to assert your lease against third parties under the Housing Lease Protection Act, and if you also obtain a fixed date stamp, you gain priority repayment rights.

moreFaqs.q: Can I request a consultation without a Korean phone number?
moreFaqs.a: Yes. You may write an international phone number or a messenger ID on the consultation request form.

moreFaqs.q: Can I get advice in Vietnamese or other languages?
moreFaqs.a: Consultations are available in English and Chinese. For other languages, we can arrange an interpreter if needed, so please let us know your preferred language when you request a consultation.

moreFaqs.q: Does a lawyer handle my case personally?
moreFaqs.a: A managing partner advises you personally and does not hide behind office managers or associate lawyers. The lawyer in charge personally sits in on questioning, visits clients, writes opinions and handles litigation.

moreFaqs.q: Are there public help lines I can use besides a lawyer?
moreFaqs.a: For general information on stay and visas, you can contact the Ministry of Justice Immigration Contact Center (dial 1345 in Korea with no area code); for labor issues such as unpaid wages, the Ministry of Employment and Labor Customer Counseling Center (dial 1350 with no area code); and for everyday legal advice, the Korea Legal Aid Corporation (132). If you have already received a decision or are in a dispute with a deadline, also get advice from a lawyer.

moreFaqs.q: Can a family member in my home country get advice on my behalf?
moreFaqs.a: A family member can get advice first to sort out the situation. However, to entrust us with the case or submit documents, authorization from the person concerned is needed, and if the person has been arrested or detained, the lawyer visits them in person to confirm their wishes.
